case_info.scenario: A 64-year-old woman was referred to our clinic for continued management of long-standing chronic rhinosinusitis without nasal polyps. Medical history included type 2 diabetes, congestive heart failure, coronary artery disease, chronic kidney disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, hypertension, obstructive sleep apnea, a 42–pack-year smoking history, and chronic rhinosinusitis for which she underwent endoscopic sinus surgery 23 years prior. Despite surgery, she had persistent, thick postnasal drip with mucopurulent drainage and was treated with saline and gentamicin rinses 10 years prior to presentation with symptomatic improvement. Imaging available from this period did not demonstrate obstructive sinus disease. The patient continued using the irrigations for the next 8 years until stopping 2 years prior to presentation. On history, the patient continued to report ongoing headaches and discolored nasal drainage bilaterally. A computed tomographic scan obtained 2 months prior to presentation for facial trauma workup demonstrated right posterior maxillary wall and ethmoid sinus changes (Figure 1). Nasal endoscopic results revealed yellow-green mucopurulent debris in the right maxillary sinus, which was sent for culture. The culture subsequently identifiedPseudomonas aeruginosa.As a result, the patient was again treated with gentamicin and budesonide nasal irrigations. Clearance of the mucopurulent debris provided an unobstructed view of the nasal mucosa during repeat endoscopy, revealing multiple outgrowths with a cobblestone appearance on the posterior walls of the maxillary sinus.
case_info.caption: Pretreatment recent axial computed tomographic imaging of the maxillary (A) and ethmoid (B) sinuses demonstrating multifocal bony abnormalities (arrowheads) with minimal mucosa edema or osteitic wall thickening.
case_info.explanation: Often seen in “surfer’s ear,” exostoses are benign bony growths commonly found in the external auditory canal (EAC).1While the exact mechanism of exostosis formation has yet to be fully elucidated, it is typically observed in patients who frequently engage in surfing or aquatic activities.1,2Literature dating back to 1938 demonstrates a relationship between prolonged and repeated water exposure, particularly cold water, and the formation of exostoses in the EAC. Kroon et al3demonstrated that each year spent surfing was associated with a 12% increased risk of developing exostosis, as well as a 10% increased risk of exostosis progression. As the periosteum of the EAC lacks the insulating protection of subcutaneous fat, it is hypothesized that cold water entering the EAC causes a periosteal insult, triggering a hyperplastic response that leads to the formation of new bone layers as a protective mechanism.4Histologically, these lesions are identified by concentric layers of lamellar bone, which likely result from repeated stimulation of the periosteum from cold temperatures.5Clinically, EAC exostoses present with a range of symptoms depending on degree of obstruction; ear fullness, trapped water, otitis externa, conductive hearing loss, and tinnitus are known complications.2Although rare, several cases of paranasal sinus exostoses (PSE) have been reported.4,6-8Similar to the EAC, the lining of the paranasal sinuses is thin and lacks an insulating layer of subcutaneous adipose tissue. Thus, it is suggested that paranasal sinus bone is similarly susceptible to temperature fluctuations and resulting periosteal reactivity.4 PSE have been described in dentistry,9,10radiology,8and otolaryngology4,6,7literature. On review of reports where otolaryngologists have been involved in the evaluation and management of PSE,4,6-8diagnosis was based on a combination of endoscopic and radiographic findings. Endoscopic examination of PSE demonstrates multiple small, oval, cystic-appearing protuberant outgrowths arranged in cobblestone patterns that are firm to instrument palpation (Figure 2). Radiographically, PSE appears as rounded, compact, radio-dense, multifocal bony outgrowths on the luminal surfaces and septa of the paranasal sinuses, without intracranial or infraorbital extension. PSE has been described in the maxillary, ethmoid, and sphenoid sinuses.4,6-8History typically reveals prior sinus surgery and the use of cold nasal irrigations, including saline or antimicrobial rinses. No cases of PSE have been reported in stenotic or obstructed sinuses, nor in association with overlying mucosal edema or inflammatory processes. Biopsies of PSE by Ramakrishnan et al4demonstrated histopathological similarities between PSE and EAC exostoses, while Haffey et al reported “benign-appearing fragments of bone, with no evidence of malignancy.”6(p1894)In all cases, no symptoms were directly attributed to PSE.4,6-8PSE were not demonstrated to further grow or develop once cold irrigations were stopped.6,7 This case demonstrated an uncommon paranasal sinus lesion in a common rhinologic clinical scenario, diagnosed through endoscopy, computed tomographic imaging, and patient history. The patient experienced resolution of her chronic rhinosinusitis symptoms with gentamicin rinses, without recurrence following the transition to saline irrigations. She was counseled on the use of warm or room temperature rinses to mitigate the risk of exostosis progression. Given the location of the exostosis, we did not believe it contributed to her history of recurrent sinusitis or posed a risk of obstructive sinus disease; therefore, surgical intervention was not indicated. Paranasal exostoses should be considered in the differential diagnosis of maxillary and ethmoid sinus lesions, and management includes cessation of cold-water irrigations and clinical monitoring.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Often seen in “surfer’s ear,” exostoses are benign bony growths commonly found in the external auditory canal (EAC).1While the exact mechanism of exostosis formation has yet to be fully elucidated, it is typically observed in patients who frequently engage in surfing or aquatic activities.1,2Literature dating back to 1938 demonstrates a relationship between prolonged and repeated water exposure, particularly cold water, and the formation of exostoses in the EAC. Kroon et al3demonstrated that each year spent surfing was associated with a 12% increased risk of developing exostosis, as well as a 10% increased risk of exostosis progression. As the periosteum of the EAC lacks the insulating protection of subcutaneous fat, it is hypothesized that cold water entering the EAC causes a periosteal insult, triggering a hyperplastic response that leads to the formation of new bone layers as a protective mechanism.4Histologically, these lesions are identified by concentric layers of lamellar bone, which likely result from repeated stimulation of the periosteum from cold temperatures.5Clinically, EAC exostoses present with a range of symptoms depending on degree of obstruction; ear fullness, trapped water, otitis externa, conductive hearing loss, and tinnitus are known complications.2Although rare, several cases of paranasal sinus exostoses (PSE) have been reported.4,6-8Similar to the EAC, the lining of the paranasal sinuses is thin and lacks an insulating layer of subcutaneous adipose tissue. Thus, it is suggested that paranasal sinus bone is similarly susceptible to temperature fluctuations and resulting periosteal reactivity.4 PSE have been described in dentistry,9,10radiology,8and otolaryngology4,6,7literature. On review of reports where otolaryngologists have been involved in the evaluation and management of PSE,4,6-8diagnosis was based on a combination of endoscopic and radiographic findings. Endoscopic examination of PSE demonstrates multiple small, oval, cystic-appearing protuberant outgrowths arranged in cobblestone patterns that are firm to instrument palpation (Figure 2). Radiographically, PSE appears as rounded, compact, radio-dense, multifocal bony outgrowths on the luminal surfaces and septa of the paranasal sinuses, without intracranial or infraorbital extension. PSE has been described in the maxillary, ethmoid, and sphenoid sinuses.4,6-8History typically reveals prior sinus surgery and the use of cold nasal irrigations, including saline or antimicrobial rinses. No cases of PSE have been reported in stenotic or obstructed sinuses, nor in association with overlying mucosal edema or inflammatory processes. Biopsies of PSE by Ramakrishnan et al4demonstrated histopathological similarities between PSE and EAC exostoses, while Haffey et al reported “benign-appearing fragments of bone, with no evidence of malignancy.”6(p1894)In all cases, no symptoms were directly attributed to PSE.4,6-8PSE were not demonstrated to further grow or develop once cold irrigations were stopped.6,7 This case demonstrated an uncommon paranasal sinus lesion in a common rhinologic clinical scenario, diagnosed through endoscopy, computed tomographic imaging, and patient history. The patient experienced resolution of her chronic rhinosinusitis symptoms with gentamicin rinses, without recurrence following the transition to saline irrigations. She was counseled on the use of warm or room temperature rinses to mitigate the risk of exostosis progression. Given the location of the exostosis, we did not believe it contributed to her history of recurrent sinusitis or posed a risk of obstructive sinus disease; therefore, surgical intervention was not indicated. Paranasal exostoses should be considered in the differential diagnosis of maxillary and ethmoid sinus lesions, and management includes cessation of cold-water irrigations and clinical monitoring.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid

case_info.explanation: Often seen in “surfer’s ear,” exostoses are benign bony growths commonly found in the external auditory canal (EAC).1While the exact mechanism of exostosis formation has yet to be fully elucidated, it is typically observed in patients who frequently engage in surfing or aquatic activities.1,2Literature dating back to 1938 demonstrates a relationship between prolonged and repeated water exposure, particularly cold water, and the formation of exostoses in the EAC. Kroon et al3demonstrated that each year spent surfing was associated with a 12% increased risk of developing exostosis, as well as a 10% increased risk of exostosis progression. As the periosteum of the EAC lacks the insulating protection of subcutaneous fat, it is hypothesized that cold water entering the EAC causes a periosteal insult, triggering a hyperplastic response that leads to the formation of new bone layers as a protective mechanism.4Histologically, these lesions are identified by concentric layers of lamellar bone, which likely result from repeated stimulation of the periosteum from cold temperatures.5Clinically, EAC exostoses present with a range of symptoms depending on degree of obstruction; ear fullness, trapped water, otitis externa, conductive hearing loss, and tinnitus are known complications.2Although rare, several cases of paranasal sinus exostoses (PSE) have been reported.4,6-8Similar to the EAC, the lining of the paranasal sinuses is thin and lacks an insulating layer of subcutaneous adipose tissue. Thus, it is suggested that paranasal sinus bone is similarly susceptible to temperature fluctuations and resulting periosteal reactivity.4 PSE have been described in dentistry,9,10radiology,8and otolaryngology4,6,7literature. On review of reports where otolaryngologists have been involved in the evaluation and management of PSE,4,6-8diagnosis was based on a combination of endoscopic and radiographic findings. Endoscopic examination of PSE demonstrates multiple small, oval, cystic-appearing protuberant outgrowths arranged in cobblestone patterns that are firm to instrument palpation (Figure 2). Radiographically, PSE appears as rounded, compact, radio-dense, multifocal bony outgrowths on the luminal surfaces and septa of the paranasal sinuses, without intracranial or infraorbital extension. PSE has been described in the maxillary, ethmoid, and sphenoid sinuses.4,6-8History typically reveals prior sinus surgery and the use of cold nasal irrigations, including saline or antimicrobial rinses. No cases of PSE have been reported in stenotic or obstructed sinuses, nor in association with overlying mucosal edema or inflammatory processes. Biopsies of PSE by Ramakrishnan et al4demonstrated histopathological similarities between PSE and EAC exostoses, while Haffey et al reported “benign-appearing fragments of bone, with no evidence of malignancy.”6(p1894)In all cases, no symptoms were directly attributed to PSE.4,6-8PSE were not demonstrated to further grow or develop once cold irrigations were stopped.6,7 This case demonstrated an uncommon paranasal sinus lesion in a common rhinologic clinical scenario, diagnosed through endoscopy, computed tomographic imaging, and patient history. The patient experienced resolution of her chronic rhinosinusitis symptoms with gentamicin rinses, without recurrence following the transition to saline irrigations. She was counseled on the use of warm or room temperature rinses to mitigate the risk of exostosis progression. Given the location of the exostosis, we did not believe it contributed to her history of recurrent sinusitis or posed a risk of obstructive sinus disease; therefore, surgical intervention was not indicated. Paranasal exostoses should be considered in the differential diagnosis of maxillary and ethmoid sinus lesions, and management includes cessation of cold-water irrigations and clinical monitoring.

case_info.explanation: Often seen in “surfer’s ear,” exostoses are benign bony growths commonly found in the external auditory canal (EAC).1While the exact mechanism of exostosis formation has yet to be fully elucidated, it is typically observed in patients who frequently engage in surfing or aquatic activities.1,2Literature dating back to 1938 demonstrates a relationship between prolonged and repeated water exposure, particularly cold water, and the formation of exostoses in the EAC. Kroon et al3demonstrated that each year spent surfing was associated with a 12% increased risk of developing exostosis, as well as a 10% increased risk of exostosis progression. As the periosteum of the EAC lacks the insulating protection of subcutaneous fat, it is hypothesized that cold water entering the EAC causes a periosteal insult, triggering a hyperplastic response that leads to the formation of new bone layers as a protective mechanism.4Histologically, these lesions are identified by concentric layers of lamellar bone, which likely result from repeated stimulation of the periosteum from cold temperatures.5Clinically, EAC exostoses present with a range of symptoms depending on degree of obstruction; ear fullness, trapped water, otitis externa, conductive hearing loss, and tinnitus are known complications.2Although rare, several cases of paranasal sinus exostoses (PSE) have been reported.4,6-8Similar to the EAC, the lining of the paranasal sinuses is thin and lacks an insulating layer of subcutaneous adipose tissue. Thus, it is suggested that paranasal sinus bone is similarly susceptible to temperature fluctuations and resulting periosteal reactivity.4 PSE have been described in dentistry,9,10radiology,8and otolaryngology4,6,7literature. On review of reports where otolaryngologists have been involved in the evaluation and management of PSE,4,6-8diagnosis was based on a combination of endoscopic and radiographic findings. Endoscopic examination of PSE demonstrates multiple small, oval, cystic-appearing protuberant outgrowths arranged in cobblestone patterns that are firm to instrument palpation (Figure 2). Radiographically, PSE appears as rounded, compact, radio-dense, multifocal bony outgrowths on the luminal surfaces and septa of the paranasal sinuses, without intracranial or infraorbital extension. PSE has been described in the maxillary, ethmoid, and sphenoid sinuses.4,6-8History typically reveals prior sinus surgery and the use of cold nasal irrigations, including saline or antimicrobial rinses. No cases of PSE have been reported in stenotic or obstructed sinuses, nor in association with overlying mucosal edema or inflammatory processes. Biopsies of PSE by Ramakrishnan et al4demonstrated histopathological similarities between PSE and EAC exostoses, while Haffey et al reported “benign-appearing fragments of bone, with no evidence of malignancy.”6(p1894)In all cases, no symptoms were directly attributed to PSE.4,6-8PSE were not demonstrated to further grow or develop once cold irrigations were stopped.6,7 This case demonstrated an uncommon paranasal sinus lesion in a common rhinologic clinical scenario, diagnosed through endoscopy, computed tomographic imaging, and patient history. The patient experienced resolution of her chronic rhinosinusitis symptoms with gentamicin rinses, without recurrence following the transition to saline irrigations. She was counseled on the use of warm or room temperature rinses to mitigate the risk of exostosis progression. Given the location of the exostosis, we did not believe it contributed to her history of recurrent sinusitis or posed a risk of obstructive sinus disease; therefore, surgical intervention was not indicated. Paranasal exostoses should be considered in the differential diagnosis of maxillary and ethmoid sinus lesions, and management includes cessation of cold-water irrigations and clinical monitoring.

Imaging available from this period did not demonstrate obstructive sinus disease. The patient continued using the irrigations for the next 8 years until stopping 2 years prior to presentation. On history, the patient continued to report ongoing headaches and discolored nasal drainage bilaterally. A computed tomographic scan obtained 2 months prior to presentation for facial trauma workup demonstrated right posterior maxillary wall and ethmoid sinus changes (Figure 1). Nasal endoscopic results revealed yellow-green mucopurulent debris in the right maxillary sinus, which was sent for culture. The culture subsequently identifiedPseudomonas aeruginosa.As a result, the patient was again treated with gentamicin and budesonide nasal irrigations. Clearance of the mucopurulent debris provided an unobstructed view of the nasal mucosa during repeat endoscopy, revealing multiple outgrowths with a cobblestone appearance on the posterior walls of the maxillary sinus.

You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

   Definition:

   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.

   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.

       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop

   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

case_info.explanation: Often seen in “surfer’s ear,” exostoses are benign bony growths commonly found in the external auditory canal (EAC).1While the exact mechanism of exostosis formation has yet to be fully elucidated, it is typically observed in patients who frequently engage in surfing or aquatic activities.1,2Literature dating back to 1938 demonstrates a relationship between prolonged and repeated water exposure, particularly cold water, and the formation of exostoses in the EAC. Kroon et al3demonstrated that each year spent surfing was associated with a 12% increased risk of developing exostosis, as well as a 10% increased risk of exostosis progression. As the periosteum of the EAC lacks the insulating protection of subcutaneous fat, it is hypothesized that cold water entering the EAC causes a periosteal insult, triggering a hyperplastic response that leads to the formation of new bone layers as a protective mechanism.4Histologically, these lesions are identified by concentric layers of lamellar bone, which likely result from repeated stimulation of the periosteum from cold temperatures.5Clinically, EAC exostoses present with a range of symptoms depending on degree of obstruction; ear fullness, trapped water, otitis externa, conductive hearing loss, and tinnitus are known complications.2Although rare, several cases of paranasal sinus exostoses (PSE) have been reported.4,6-8Similar to the EAC, the lining of the paranasal sinuses is thin and lacks an insulating layer of subcutaneous adipose tissue. Thus, it is suggested that paranasal sinus bone is similarly susceptible to temperature fluctuations and resulting periosteal reactivity.4 PSE have been described in dentistry,9,10radiology,8and otolaryngology4,6,7literature. On review of reports where otolaryngologists have been involved in the evaluation and management of PSE,4,6-8diagnosis was based on a combination of endoscopic and radiographic findings. Endoscopic examination of PSE demonstrates multiple small, oval, cystic-appearing protuberant outgrowths arranged in cobblestone patterns that are firm to instrument palpation (Figure 2). Radiographically, PSE appears as rounded, compact, radio-dense, multifocal bony outgrowths on the luminal surfaces and septa of the paranasal sinuses, without intracranial or infraorbital extension. PSE has been described in the maxillary, ethmoid, and sphenoid sinuses.4,6-8History typically reveals prior sinus surgery and the use of cold nasal irrigations, including saline or antimicrobial rinses. No cases of PSE have been reported in stenotic or obstructed sinuses, nor in association with overlying mucosal edema or inflammatory processes. Biopsies of PSE by Ramakrishnan et al4demonstrated histopathological similarities between PSE and EAC exostoses, while Haffey et al reported “benign-appearing fragments of bone, with no evidence of malignancy.”6(p1894)In all cases, no symptoms were directly attributed to PSE.4,6-8PSE were not demonstrated to further grow or develop once cold irrigations were stopped.6,7 This case demonstrated an uncommon paranasal sinus lesion in a common rhinologic clinical scenario, diagnosed through endoscopy, computed tomographic imaging, and patient history. The patient experienced resolution of her chronic rhinosinusitis symptoms with gentamicin rinses, without recurrence following the transition to saline irrigations. She was counseled on the use of warm or room temperature rinses to mitigate the risk of exostosis progression. Given the location of the exostosis, we did not believe it contributed to her history of recurrent sinusitis or posed a risk of obstructive sinus disease; therefore, surgical intervention was not indicated. Paranasal exostoses should be considered in the differential diagnosis of maxillary and ethmoid sinus lesions, and management includes cessation of cold-water irrigations and clinical monitoring.

case_info.explanation: Often seen in “surfer’s ear,” exostoses are benign bony growths commonly found in the external auditory canal (EAC).1While the exact mechanism of exostosis formation has yet to be fully elucidated, it is typically observed in patients who frequently engage in surfing or aquatic activities.1,2Literature dating back to 1938 demonstrates a relationship between prolonged and repeated water exposure, particularly cold water, and the formation of exostoses in the EAC. Kroon et al3demonstrated that each year spent surfing was associated with a 12% increased risk of developing exostosis, as well as a 10% increased risk of exostosis progression. As the periosteum of the EAC lacks the insulating protection of subcutaneous fat, it is hypothesized that cold water entering the EAC causes a periosteal insult, triggering a hyperplastic response that leads to the formation of new bone layers as a protective mechanism.4Histologically, these lesions are identified by concentric layers of lamellar bone, which likely result from repeated stimulation of the periosteum from cold temperatures.5Clinically, EAC exostoses present with a range of symptoms depending on degree of obstruction; ear fullness, trapped water, otitis externa, conductive hearing loss, and tinnitus are known complications.2Although rare, several cases of paranasal sinus exostoses (PSE) have been reported.4,6-8Similar to the EAC, the lining of the paranasal sinuses is thin and lacks an insulating layer of subcutaneous adipose tissue. Thus, it is suggested that paranasal sinus bone is similarly susceptible to temperature fluctuations and resulting periosteal reactivity.4 PSE have been described in dentistry,9,10radiology,8and otolaryngology4,6,7literature. On review of reports where otolaryngologists have been involved in the evaluation and management of PSE,4,6-8diagnosis was based on a combination of endoscopic and radiographic findings. Endoscopic examination of PSE demonstrates multiple small, oval, cystic-appearing protuberant outgrowths arranged in cobblestone patterns that are firm to instrument palpation (Figure 2). Radiographically, PSE appears as rounded, compact, radio-dense, multifocal bony outgrowths on the luminal surfaces and septa of the paranasal sinuses, without intracranial or infraorbital extension. PSE has been described in the maxillary, ethmoid, and sphenoid sinuses.4,6-8History typically reveals prior sinus surgery and the use of cold nasal irrigations, including saline or antimicrobial rinses. No cases of PSE have been reported in stenotic or obstructed sinuses, nor in association with overlying mucosal edema or inflammatory processes. Biopsies of PSE by Ramakrishnan et al4demonstrated histopathological similarities between PSE and EAC exostoses, while Haffey et al reported “benign-appearing fragments of bone, with no evidence of malignancy.”6(p1894)In all cases, no symptoms were directly attributed to PSE.4,6-8PSE were not demonstrated to further grow or develop once cold irrigations were stopped.6,7 This case demonstrated an uncommon paranasal sinus lesion in a common rhinologic clinical scenario, diagnosed through endoscopy, computed tomographic imaging, and patient history. The patient experienced resolution of her chronic rhinosinusitis symptoms with gentamicin rinses, without recurrence following the transition to saline irrigations. She was counseled on the use of warm or room temperature rinses to mitigate the risk of exostosis progression. Given the location of the exostosis, we did not believe it contributed to her history of recurrent sinusitis or posed a risk of obstructive sinus disease; therefore, surgical intervention was not indicated. Paranasal exostoses should be considered in the differential diagnosis of maxillary and ethmoid sinus lesions, and management includes cessation of cold-water irrigations and clinical monitoring.

      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,

  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid

   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Often seen in “surfer’s ear,” exostoses are benign bony growths commonly found in the external auditory canal (EAC).1While the exact mechanism of exostosis formation has yet to be fully elucidated, it is typically observed in patients who frequently engage in surfing or aquatic activities.1,2Literature dating back to 1938 demonstrates a relationship between prolonged and repeated water exposure, particularly cold water, and the formation of exostoses in the EAC. Kroon et al3demonstrated that each year spent surfing was associated with a 12% increased risk of developing exostosis, as well as a 10% increased risk of exostosis progression. As the periosteum of the EAC lacks the insulating protection of subcutaneous fat, it is hypothesized that cold water entering the EAC causes a periosteal insult, triggering a hyperplastic response that leads to the formation of new bone layers as a protective mechanism.4Histologically, these lesions are identified by concentric layers of lamellar bone, which likely result from repeated stimulation of the periosteum from cold temperatures.5Clinically, EAC exostoses present with a range of symptoms depending on degree of obstruction; ear fullness, trapped water, otitis externa, conductive hearing loss, and tinnitus are known complications.2Although rare, several cases of paranasal sinus exostoses (PSE) have been reported.4,6-8Similar to the EAC, the lining of the paranasal sinuses is thin and lacks an insulating layer of subcutaneous adipose tissue. Thus, it is suggested that paranasal sinus bone is similarly susceptible to temperature fluctuations and resulting periosteal reactivity.4 PSE have been described in dentistry,9,10radiology,8and otolaryngology4,6,7literature. On review of reports where otolaryngologists have been involved in the evaluation and management of PSE,4,6-8diagnosis was based on a combination of endoscopic and radiographic findings. Endoscopic examination of PSE demonstrates multiple small, oval, cystic-appearing protuberant outgrowths arranged in cobblestone patterns that are firm to instrument palpation (Figure 2). Radiographically, PSE appears as rounded, compact, radio-dense, multifocal bony outgrowths on the luminal surfaces and septa of the paranasal sinuses, without intracranial or infraorbital extension. PSE has been described in the maxillary, ethmoid, and sphenoid sinuses.4,6-8History typically reveals prior sinus surgery and the use of cold nasal irrigations, including saline or antimicrobial rinses. No cases of PSE have been reported in stenotic or obstructed sinuses, nor in association with overlying mucosal edema or inflammatory processes. Biopsies of PSE by Ramakrishnan et al4demonstrated histopathological similarities between PSE and EAC exostoses, while Haffey et al reported “benign-appearing fragments of bone, with no evidence of malignancy.”6(p1894)In all cases, no symptoms were directly attributed to PSE.4,6-8PSE were not demonstrated to further grow or develop once cold irrigations were stopped.6,7 This case demonstrated an uncommon paranasal sinus lesion in a common rhinologic clinical scenario, diagnosed through endoscopy, computed tomographic imaging, and patient history. The patient experienced resolution of her chronic rhinosinusitis symptoms with gentamicin rinses, without recurrence following the transition to saline irrigations. She was counseled on the use of warm or room temperature rinses to mitigate the risk of exostosis progression. Given the location of the exostosis, we did not believe it contributed to her history of recurrent sinusitis or posed a risk of obstructive sinus disease; therefore, surgical intervention was not indicated. Paranasal exostoses should be considered in the differential diagnosis of maxillary and ethmoid sinus lesions, and management includes cessation of cold-water irrigations and clinical monitoring.

A 64-year-old woman was referred to our clinic for continued management of long-standing chronic rhinosinusitis without nasal polyps. Imaging available from this period did not demonstrate obstructive sinus disease. The patient continued using the irrigations for the next 8 years until stopping 2 years prior to presentation. On history, the patient continued to report ongoing headaches and discolored nasal drainage bilaterally. A computed tomographic scan obtained 2 months prior to presentation for facial trauma workup demonstrated right posterior maxillary wall and ethmoid sinus changes (Figure 1). Nasal endoscopic results revealed yellow-green mucopurulent debris in the right maxillary sinus, which was sent for culture. The culture subsequently identifiedPseudomonas aeruginosa.As a result, the patient was again treated with gentamicin and budesonide nasal irrigations. Clearance of the mucopurulent debris provided an unobstructed view of the nasal mucosa during repeat endoscopy, revealing multiple outgrowths with a cobblestone appearance on the posterior walls of the maxillary sinus.

You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

[Behavior Guideline]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.

   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple

       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Often seen in “surfer’s ear,” exostoses are benign bony growths commonly found in the external auditory canal (EAC).1While the exact mechanism of exostosis formation has yet to be fully elucidated, it is typically observed in patients who frequently engage in surfing or aquatic activities.1,2Literature dating back to 1938 demonstrates a relationship between prolonged and repeated water exposure, particularly cold water, and the formation of exostoses in the EAC. Kroon et al3demonstrated that each year spent surfing was associated with a 12% increased risk of developing exostosis, as well as a 10% increased risk of exostosis progression. As the periosteum of the EAC lacks the insulating protection of subcutaneous fat, it is hypothesized that cold water entering the EAC causes a periosteal insult, triggering a hyperplastic response that leads to the formation of new bone layers as a protective mechanism.4Histologically, these lesions are identified by concentric layers of lamellar bone, which likely result from repeated stimulation of the periosteum from cold temperatures.5Clinically, EAC exostoses present with a range of symptoms depending on degree of obstruction; ear fullness, trapped water, otitis externa, conductive hearing loss, and tinnitus are known complications.2Although rare, several cases of paranasal sinus exostoses (PSE) have been reported.4,6-8Similar to the EAC, the lining of the paranasal sinuses is thin and lacks an insulating layer of subcutaneous adipose tissue. Thus, it is suggested that paranasal sinus bone is similarly susceptible to temperature fluctuations and resulting periosteal reactivity.4 PSE have been described in dentistry,9,10radiology,8and otolaryngology4,6,7literature. On review of reports where otolaryngologists have been involved in the evaluation and management of PSE,4,6-8diagnosis was based on a combination of endoscopic and radiographic findings. Endoscopic examination of PSE demonstrates multiple small, oval, cystic-appearing protuberant outgrowths arranged in cobblestone patterns that are firm to instrument palpation (Figure 2). Radiographically, PSE appears as rounded, compact, radio-dense, multifocal bony outgrowths on the luminal surfaces and septa of the paranasal sinuses, without intracranial or infraorbital extension. PSE has been described in the maxillary, ethmoid, and sphenoid sinuses.4,6-8History typically reveals prior sinus surgery and the use of cold nasal irrigations, including saline or antimicrobial rinses. No cases of PSE have been reported in stenotic or obstructed sinuses, nor in association with overlying mucosal edema or inflammatory processes. Biopsies of PSE by Ramakrishnan et al4demonstrated histopathological similarities between PSE and EAC exostoses, while Haffey et al reported “benign-appearing fragments of bone, with no evidence of malignancy.”6(p1894)In all cases, no symptoms were directly attributed to PSE.4,6-8PSE were not demonstrated to further grow or develop once cold irrigations were stopped.6,7 This case demonstrated an uncommon paranasal sinus lesion in a common rhinologic clinical scenario, diagnosed through endoscopy, computed tomographic imaging, and patient history. The patient experienced resolution of her chronic rhinosinusitis symptoms with gentamicin rinses, without recurrence following the transition to saline irrigations. She was counseled on the use of warm or room temperature rinses to mitigate the risk of exostosis progression. Given the location of the exostosis, we did not believe it contributed to her history of recurrent sinusitis or posed a risk of obstructive sinus disease; therefore, surgical intervention was not indicated. Paranasal exostoses should be considered in the differential diagnosis of maxillary and ethmoid sinus lesions, and management includes cessation of cold-water irrigations and clinical monitoring.
